title: What do O, Omega and Theta actually mean?
source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: What does f(n)=O(g(n)) assert for eventually nonnegative functions?
options: The same running time on every input
qs.why: There must be fixed c>0 and n0 with f(n)≤c g(n) for all n≥n0.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: Which notation requires both an eventual upper and lower constant-factor bound?
qs.why: Θ combines O and Ω for the same comparison function.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: For f(n)=3n²+7n+4, which term determines its tight growth class?
qs.why: For n≥1 all lower terms are bounded by constants times n²; the quadratic term supplies a lower bound.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: Can constants c and n0 depend on n in a Big-O proof?
options: Both may vary with every input
Only c may depend on n
Only n0 may depend on n
qs.why: The quantifier order chooses constants before requiring the inequality for every sufficiently large n.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: For n≥1, which pair witnesses 3n²+7n+4∈Θ(n²)?
qs.why: Use n≤n² and 1≤n² to obtain the upper coefficient 3+7+4=14.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: A worst-case cost W(n) is Θ(n²). Which statement must hold?
qs.why: For n≥1, n²≤n³; an upper bound need not be tight. Worst-case information does not determine every input.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: If f∈O(g) and g∈O(h), which implication follows?
qs.why: Multiply the two fixed upper-bound constants and take the larger threshold.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a bound from a case?
qs.correct: O is an upper bound; worst case selects a cost function
options: Ω means best case by definition
O is an upper bound; worst case selects a cost function
O means worst case by definition
Θ means average case by definition
qs.why: One can give O, Ω or Θ bounds on best-, average- or worst-case functions.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: Let f(n)=n² for even n and n for odd n. What is true relative to n²?
qs.why: On odd n, f/n²=1/n tends to zero, preventing a positive eventual lower constant.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: For f(n)=n and g(n)=n(2+sin n), what tight relation holds for n≥1?
options: f grows strictly faster than g
qs.why: Since 1≤2+sin n≤3, g/3≤f≤g despite oscillation.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: For f(n)=n² and g(n)=n³, which combination is true?
qs.why: The ratio f/g=1/n tends to zero; upper and reverse lower bounds hold, but not tight equivalence.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: If f,g are eventually positive and f∈Θ(g), what follows?
options: Their exact operation counts are equal
qs.why: Invert the two positive constant inequalities; Θ is symmetric, exact equality is unnecessary.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

qs.stem: Malfoid sees an O(n²) upper bound and declares the algorithm cannot be linear. What is wrong?
qs.correct: A linear function also satisfies O(n²)
options: A linear function also satisfies O(n²)
Only constants can have multiple upper bounds
qs.why: An upper bound alone does not establish a matching lower bound; n≤n² for n≥1.
qs.source: Analysis Techniques pp5–12; Review Week 8 pp2–3; study notes 01-analysis §§1.1–1.2.
qs.context: Functions are eventually nonnegative, n is a positive integer, and asymptotic constants are fixed independently of n.

n log n and n² have identical leading terms

title: What are P and NP, and what does verification mean?
source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5. Matching later recordings unavailable; approved slides-and-notes grounding.
context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What kind of problems are formally classified by P and NP here?
qs.why: The formal definitions concern yes/no membership languages.

qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What does P require?
options: Only fast yes answers without no answers
A short program regardless of runtime
qs.why: A decider must correctly answer both yes and no within a polynomial input-length bound.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What does NP verification require for yes instances?
qs.correct: A polynomial-length certificate checked by a polynomial-time verifier
options: A certificate for every no instance under the same definition
A polynomial-length certificate checked by a polynomial-time verifier
A random guess accepted without checking
qs.why: The witness length and checking time are both bounded polynomially in the encoded instance size.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: Which inclusion is known from the definitions?
qs.why: A polynomial decider can serve as a verifier that ignores the certificate.

qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What does NP stand for?
qs.why: NP is not defined as the set of problems outside polynomial time.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: A TSP tour certificate lists a permutation of vertices. What must a verifier check beyond its cost?
qs.correct: Every vertex appears exactly once and the closing tour is valid
options: Only that all labels are integers
Every vertex appears exactly once and the closing tour is valid
qs.why: The certificate must meet the full feasibility predicate, including returning to the start.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: Why does rejecting one proposed certificate not prove an NP instance is no?
qs.why: Yes means there exists a valid witness; one failed candidate does not negate that existential claim.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: Does easy verification automatically give an easy deterministic search over all certificates?
qs.correct: No; the candidate space may be exponential
options: No; the candidate space may be exponential
Yes because the verifier ignores input
Yes; try every certificate in polynomial time
qs.why: Polynomial witness length permits exponentially many possible witnesses; checking one is different from finding one.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: A verifier accepts every input on certificate0. Why is it invalid for a nontrivial language with no instances?

options: It lacks soundness: no instances receive an accepted certificate

qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: A verifier rejects all certificates for one actual yes instance. Which requirement fails?
qs.why: Every yes instance must have at least one accepted witness.

qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: If certificates of length polynomial in |x| are allowed but checking them can take 2^|x| time, is NP membership proved?
qs.correct: No; polynomial verification time is also required
options: No; polynomial verification time is also required
Yes if the verifier eventually halts
qs.why: Both bounds are required, measured against the encoded input size with a polynomially bounded witness.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: What would a proof that one language in NP is outside P establish?

qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

qs.stem: Malfoid says NP problems have no polynomial algorithm because NP means non-polynomial. What is wrong?
qs.correct: NP includes P, and the abbreviation has a different meaning
options: NP includes P, and the abbreviation has a different meaning
Every NP problem is known exponential
qs.why: The definition is nondeterministic polynomial time; it does not assert deterministic hardness of every member.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp9–19; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §§8.3–8.5.
qs.context: P and NP refer to decision languages measured in encoded input length. Use the full feasibility predicate when checking a proposed certificate.

title: Which direction does a polynomial reduction go?

qs.stem: What does A≤pB mean in the many-one model used here?
qs.correct: A instances map in polynomial time to equivalent B instances
options: A and B have identical inputs
A is faster on every measured input
A instances map in polynomial time to equivalent B instances
qs.why: There is one polynomial function f with x∈A iff f(x)∈B.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: Given A≤pB and a polynomial-time solver for B, what follows?
options: B must be harder than every language
qs.why: Compute f(x), run the B solver and return its yes/no answer.

qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: To prove a proposed target B hard using known-hard A, which direction is needed?
qs.why: An efficient B algorithm must then solve the known-hard source A.

qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: What logical relationship must a many-one reduction preserve?
qs.why: Both directions are necessary to preserve no instances as well.

qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: If A≤pB and B≤pC, what follows?
qs.why: Compose the polynomial transformations; output size is also polynomially bounded.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: If A≤pB and A is easy, does that prove B easy?
qs.why: An easy source may reduce to a much harder target; the solver implication goes from target to source.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: If A≤pB and B∈P, which result follows?
qs.why: Polynomial transformation followed by polynomial solving remains polynomial.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: If A≤pB and A∉P, what can be concluded about B?
options: A and B must have equal runtime
qs.why: Otherwise a polynomial B solver would yield a polynomial A solver, contradicting A∉P.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: A construction proves only x∈A⇒f(x)∈B. What is missing?
options: Prove the function has a shorter name
Prove every B instance is an output
qs.why: Without the reverse implication, no instances could map to yes instances and the answer would be unsound.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: Why must reduction runtime include the size of its constructed instance?
qs.correct: Writing the output must also fit polynomial time
options: Only the source certificate is measured
Writing the output must also fit polynomial time
A reduction may write infinitely many symbols
qs.why: A polynomial-time explicit construction cannot produce a superpolynomial-length output.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: Does an algorithm using several adaptive calls to B automatically constitute one many-one reduction A≤pB?
qs.correct: No; that is a different reduction model unless converted
options: No; that is a different reduction model unless converted
No reduction may use any solver conceptually
qs.why: A many-one proof needs a single transformed instance with an iff condition; an oracle-use illustration alone is insufficient.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: A known NP-complete problem A reduces to B, but B∈NP has not been proved. What is still missing before calling B NP-complete?
options: A proof that B has no algorithm
qs.why: Hardness and membership are separate obligations.
qs.source: Introduction to NP pp20–23; study notes 08-np-and-heuristics §8.6.
qs.context: Use deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, denoted A≤pB. Keep source and target roles distinct; both logical directions must be considered.

qs.stem: Malfoid proves B≤pA for known-hard A and calls B hard. What is the correction?
qs.correct: That direction shows B is no harder than A; hardness needs A≤pB
options: Any arrow involving A proves B hard
That direction shows B is no harder than A; hardness needs A≤pB
qs.why: A solver for A can solve B under the given direction, which does not establish difficulty of B.

Every accepted target tour can be broken into an original HP as well as every HP being closable
